event: Billy Sunday mine, in the same quarter section as the Clipper, mines 1,900 tons of ore from stopes above the 120 ft level.
source: USGS ARDF FB064 (USGS 2001, OFR 01-426), citing Hill 1933
locator: printed p. 140, Geologic description; p. 141, Production notes
notes: ARDF puts both Billy Sunday (FB064) and Clipper (FB047) in the SE1/4SW1/4 sec. 32, T. 1 N., R. 2 W.

event: Initial development work at the Clipper begins.
source: DGGS OFR 157 (Bundtzen and others, 1982)
locator: p. 1 (PDF p. 5), History of the property
notes: OFR 157 says most of its history came from conversations with G.P. Lounsbury.

event: A 235 to 250 ft drift has been driven on a thin, steep vein at the Clipper.
source: USGS ARDF FB047, citing Hill 1933 and Pilgrim 1931 to 1933; also DGGS OFR 157
locator: ARDF printed p. 101 and p. 102; OFR 157 p. 1
notes: OFR 157 says it is unclear whether this early drift is part of the workings mapped in 1982 or part of older caved workings about 60 vertical ft above the portal.

event: Most of these early workings were mined by hand by the owner at the time, Lloyd Lounsbury.
source: D. Wietchy, oral communication, 2000, as cited in USGS ARDF FB047
notes: Who D. Wietchy is is not stated in the ARDF. Conflict: Reed 1938 (printed pp. 8 to 9) names seven other owners and says the mine was under lease to Lloyd P. Lounsbury. Both are kept. See the 1938 row and OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.

event: About 19 tons of ore are produced, with an average value of $28 to $30 a ton.
source: Reed, Lode Mining and Development in the Year 1938, the Fairbanks District, Alaska, Territory of Alaska Department of Mines (DGGS Miscellaneous Report 194-6); also DGGS OFR 157 and USGS ARDF FB047
locator: Reed printed p. 9 (PDF p. 10); OFR 157 p. 3 (PDF p. 7); ARDF printed p. 102, Production notes
notes: Corrected 28 Nov 2026. Reed gives dollars a ton and says produced. OFR 157 restates this as about 0.8 oz gold per ton, milled, and the ARDF credits the 0.8 oz figure to Reed. Reed page checked by eye.

event: About 25 tons of ore are produced, at the same value.
source: Reed, Lode Mining and Development in the Year 1938, the Fairbanks District, Alaska, Territory of Alaska Department of Mines (DGGS Miscellaneous Report 194-6); also DGGS OFR 157 and USGS ARDF FB047
locator: Reed printed p. 9 (PDF p. 10); OFR 157 p. 3 (PDF p. 7); ARDF printed p. 102, Production notes
notes: Corrected 28 Nov 2026. See the 1937 row.

event: The mine's best years: about 1,400 oz of gold, worth $50,000, from hand-sorted high-grade ore.
source: G.P. Lounsbury, as told to Bundtzen and others, DGGS OFR 157; repeated in USGS ARDF FB047
locator: OFR 157 p. 3 (PDF p. 7); ARDF printed p. 101 and p. 102
notes: OFR 157 says its stope volume estimates and assays support this level of production. No mill, mint or smelter record on file confirms the figure. See OPEN-QUESTIONS.md, Production.

event: Lloyd Lounsbury, father of G.P. Lounsbury, processes the ore at the mine site with a Blake jaw crusher and a 10 ton per day Straub ball mill.
source: G.P. Lounsbury, as told to Bundtzen and others, DGGS OFR 157
notes: OFR 157 gives no exact years for the mill; it follows the 1937 to 1942 sentence. Not a stamp mill. Reed 1938 (printed p. 9) records a Blake type jaw crusher and a 10-ton Straub ball mill on the property in 1938.

event: USGS Fairbanks (D-3) topographic map, 1949 edition, made from aerial photographs taken August 1949.
source: USGS Fairbanks (D-3) quadrangle, 1949
locator: map margin, lower left and lower right

event: Earliest borough aerial photo of the site in our files.
source: FNSB (Fairbanks North Star Borough) 1949 imagery
locator: FNSB 1949 imagery layer (not in repo; terms not yet checked)
notes: Year from the borough imagery layer name. A 1938 window was checked and has no coverage.

event: Film clip, "Buildings and streets at Ester," color and silent, shows Ester in winter. It is in the George Lounsbury Collection.
source: UAF (University of Alaska Fairbanks) Alaska and Polar Regions Collections and Archives, AAF-1869
notes: It shows Ester town. It does not show the mine. Who filmed it is not stated.

event: Guided tours of the mine and mill are offered to tourists and the public.
source: G.P. Lounsbury, as told to Bundtzen and others, DGGS OFR 157

event: D. Stevens, D. Hawkins and R.B. Forbes map gold anomalies and magnetometer profile data on Ester Dome.
source: Stevens, Hawkins and Forbes 1969, Ester Dome area map
notes: The map shows sec. 32 but does not label the Clipper. No publisher is printed. File held out of the repo until the publisher is known.

event: Columbia University contract F44620-70-C-0038 takes effect, under ARPA (Advanced Research Projects Agency) Order 1513, for the Long-Period Seismological Research Program. Amount $942,578. Expires 15 Mar 1971.
source: Lamont 1971, Fairbanks installation report (DTIC AD0729918)
notes: Sponsoring military activity on the report form: Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR), PDF p. 3. The contract covers the whole program, not Fairbanks alone.

event: A Lamont-Doherty crew installs a high-gain, long-period seismograph station in the "Old Clipper Mine." Crew: Merrill Conner, Shannon Cory, Tracy Johnson and Andrew J. Murphy.
source: Lamont 1971, Fairbanks installation report (DTIC AD0729918)
notes: The last digit of each year is faint in the scan. 1970 fits the report date (31 Mar 1971) and the contract dates.

event: The report names the station manager as Lloyd Lounsbury, and the station attendants as Herbert Mann and George Lounsbury.
source: Lamont 1971, Fairbanks installation report (DTIC AD0729918)
locator: report p. 1 (PDF p. 7); Acknowledgments, report p. 42 (PDF p. 49)

event: The station sits in a side tunnel about 130 m from the mine entrance under 20 m of rock. The side tunnel is enlarged and split into four rooms: seismometer chamber, phototube amplifier room, photographic recording room and console room. Two ship-type bulkhead doors seal the instruments.
source: Lamont 1971, Fairbanks installation report (DTIC AD0729918)
locator: report p. 11 (PDF p. 18); p. 30 (PDF p. 37), item 5

event: The installation report says the mine "has not been actively worked for a number of years and is presently being used as a tourist attraction."
source: Lamont 1971, Fairbanks installation report (DTIC AD0729918)
notes: The report also prints the station position as 64 53 58 N, 148 00 20 W, 330 m. See OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.

event: Operations contract F44620-71-C-0082, $295,000, ARPA Order 1774, Columbia University.
source: Lamont 1972, annual report (DTIC AD0744130)
locator: program page, PDF p. 5; Fairbanks (FBK) listed among the stations, PDF p. 7
notes: The contract covers the whole program of stations. It is not a Fairbanks-only figure.

event: A two-man Lamont team closes the Fairbanks station, FBK. All the equipment, including the instrument tanks, is crated and shipped to NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) at Albuquerque.
source: Lamont 1973, annual report (DTIC AD0760585); also Lamont 1972, semi-annual report (DTIC AD0751960)
locator: report p. 5 (PDF p. 11); AD0751960 report p. 2 (PDF p. 8)
notes: The same sentence is printed legibly in AD0751960 and was checked by eye there.

event: "The final recordings from FBK are dated 25 April 1972."
source: Lamont 1973, annual report (DTIC AD0760585); also Lamont 1972, semi-annual report (DTIC AD0751960)
locator: report p. 5 (PDF p. 11); AD0751960 report p. 2 (PDF p. 8)
notes: Read by eye from the page image; the text layer is garbled. The same sentence is printed legibly in AD0751960 and was checked by eye there.

event: Bundtzen, Robinson, Kline and Albanese spend 7 person-days mapping about 800 ft of underground workings at the Clipper by compass and tape.
source: DGGS OFR 157 (Bundtzen and others, 1982)
notes: The report is dated July 1982.

event: The 1982 mine map labels a side drift "Lamont-Doherty Seismograph Station (Abandoned)" with "Steel Doors."
source: DGGS OFR 157 Plate 1
locator: Plate 1, station label; maps/DGGS 1982, Plate 1 crop

event: G.P. Lounsbury is the mine owner.
source: DGGS OFR 157; USGS ARDF FB047
locator: OFR 157 p. 1 (PDF p. 5); ARDF printed p. 101

event: G.P. Lounsbury sinks a 9 by 22 by 4 ft winze about 120 ft from the portal and recovers rich free-milling gold ore.
source: G.P. Lounsbury, as told to Bundtzen and others, DGGS OFR 157

event: George Lounsbury is interviewed by David Krupa for the Gates of the Arctic National Park oral history project. The interview is about Wiseman, not the Clipper.
source: UAF Oral History Program, Project Jukebox, Oral History 93-15-59
notes: In a machine transcript, the tape does not mention the Clipper or the station.

event: The BLM (Bureau of Land Management) certifies the plat of Mineral Survey No. 2493, Grass Valley (lode), claim of James G. and George H. Lounsbury. It shows a shaft, spring, cabin, outbuilding, stripping area, road and power line.
source: USMS (US Mineral Survey) 2493 Grass Valley plat
locator: certification block, lower right; title block; stamps on the left and right margins
notes: Corrected 28 Nov 2026. This row used to date the plat 2001 and call 50-2001-0164 a recording number. The certification date is handwritten: the day reads 20 or 26, the year 1988 is clear. The survey dates are not readable in our scan. The plat is stamped BK 01244 PG 0923, a recorder's book and page, and 50-2001-0164, which matches the patent serial in the 21 Dec 2000 row.

event: The USGS (US Geological Survey) Alaska Resource Data File record for the Clipper (FB047) is last updated.
source: USGS ARDF FB047

event: Borough aerial photo of the site.
source: FNSB 2007 imagery
locator: FNSB 2007 imagery layer (not in repo; terms not yet checked)
notes: Year from the borough imagery layer name.

event: Clutch and Lorna Lounsbury host a car club picnic at their Clipper Mine property. On tours into the mine, the club is shown the room of the mine's "once top secret mission."
source: Nash's News, Aug 2013, Vernon L. Nash Antique Auto Club
notes: The newsletter does not use the word station. Our reading: the room is the old station room. The newsletter also calls the Clipper "the last patented mine in Alaska"; no other source supports that.

event: Bare-earth LiDAR (laser scanning) survey of the area.
source: FNSB and USGS 2017 bare-earth LiDAR
locator: source data used for the model terrain; not in the repo

event: The Mining History Association lode mine tour visits "the Clipper Mine near Ester Dome," described as a small family-owned underground mine.
source: Mining History Association, 2017 tour photo page

event: Borough aerial photo of the site, 3 inch resolution.
source: FNSB 2023 imagery
locator: FNSB 2023 3 inch mosaic (not in repo; terms not yet checked)
notes: FNSB 2023 3 inch mosaic.

event: USGS Fairbanks D-3 SE topographic map, 2024 edition.
source: USGS US Topo, Fairbanks D-3 SE, 2024

event: A USGS report describes the Clipper as a winding tunnel about 500 ft long on the east fork of Eva Creek, at an altitude of 1,050 ft, and says "The property is worked by Lloyd Lounsbury."
source: Killeen and Mertie, Antimony ore in the Fairbanks district, Alaska, USGS Open-File Report 51-46, 1951
notes: The sentence naming Lloyd Lounsbury is bracketed by hand in the typescript but still legible. OFR 157 gives 1,100 ft. Our reading: a normal gap for map-read elevations of the time.

event: Very small waves from Rainier, an underground nuclear shot in Nevada, are found on the Coast and Geodetic Survey seismogram at College, Alaska, 3,600 km away. Stations in the eastern US at 2,000 to 3,000 km did not pick it up.
source: Surface Motions from an Underground Explosion, June 1958 (DTIC AD0607639)
notes: College is the University town, about 11 km from the Clipper. This is not the Clipper.

event: A federal Panel on Seismic Improvement, chaired by Lloyd V. Berkner, meets in Washington on better ways to detect nuclear tests. Members include Jack E. Oliver of Lamont Geological Observatory, Frank Press of Caltech and Carl F. Romney of the US Air Force.
source: Report of the Panel on Seismic Improvement, 7 Jan 1959, with cover memo of 12 Jan 1959. CIA Reading Room CIA-RDP80B01676R004300120011-2
locator: cover memo, member list; report para. 1
notes: Marked Confidential; declassified in part in 2012. It does not mention Alaska or the Clipper.

event: Lamont finishes installing a strain seismograph 1,850 ft below the surface in the Sterling Mine of the New Jersey Zinc Company, Ogdensburg, New Jersey, in an unused exploratory drift.
source: Alsop, Sutton and Ewing, Free Oscillations of the Earth Observed on Strain and Pendulum Seismographs, Journal of Geophysical Research 66(2), Feb 1961
notes: The article says the install was finished "a few months before" the Chile earthquake of 22 May 1960.

event: The University's Geophysical Institute finishes a two-story observatory on Ester Dome, 10 miles west of the campus at about 2,500 ft, for aurora and airglow studies.
source: Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska, Annual Report 1962-63
locator: PDF p. 12; photo caption PDF p. 17
notes: Near the summit. The Clipper portal is about 1,100 ft on the south side. Not the mine.

event: John B. (Jack) Townshend becomes chief of the Coast and Geodetic Survey's College Magnetic and Seismological Observatory.
source: UAF Centennial profile of Jack Townshend; Ned Rozell, UAF news, 6 Sept 2012

event: University President W. R. Wood invites Maurice Ewing, director of Lamont Geological Observatory, to join the Geophysical Institute's Advisory Committee. He agrees.
source: Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska, Annual Report 1962-63

event: Lamont's long-period seismograph station at College, Alaska, starts recording, on magnetic tape and film. Listed at 64 54 00 N, 147 47 36 W.
source: Pomeroy, Establishment of a long-period seismograph network utilizing magnetic tape recording, Lamont, 1 June 1965 (DTIC AD0622794)
notes: Footnote: start delayed "pending completion of vault construction by the cooperating station." Our reading: the position is the College Observatory, about 11 km from the Clipper.

event: The Geophysical Institute starts a seismology program. Noise studies to choose station sites use "equipment obtained on loan from the Lamont Geological Observatory."
source: Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska, Annual Report 1963-64
notes: The report does not say where the noise studies were run.

event: Jurgen Kienle spends two years at Lamont-Doherty, then joins the Geophysical Institute on 1 Jul 1970.
source: Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska, Annual Report 1969-70
notes: No document says he had any part in choosing the Clipper.

event: Lamont tests seismometers in the Ogdensburg mine in chambers behind two and three bulkhead doors, and sets the rule for new stations: instrument tanks in an air-tight vault with a bulkhead door.
source: Ward and Hade, Design and Deployment of Five High-Gain, Broad-Band, Long-Period Seismograph Stations, Lamont-Doherty, 28 Aug 1970 (DTIC AD0730950)
notes: Noise plot for June 1969. The Clipper station was later sealed behind two bulkhead doors (Lamont 1971, report p. 11).

event: A Lamont report on five new high-gain stations lists the Fairbanks site as the "Old Clipper Gold Mine with 130 meters overburden," owned by Lloyd Lounsbury (spelled "Loundsbury"). Principal contact: John B. Townshend, Chief, College Observatory.
source: Ward and Hade, Design and Deployment of Five High-Gain, Broad-Band, Long-Period Seismograph Stations, Lamont-Doherty, 28 Aug 1970 (DTIC AD0730950)
locator: report p. 7, Summary of new station sites
notes: Same contract as the install, F44620-70-C-0038. Phone numbers printed on the page are left out here. Its depth, longitude and elevation differ from the 1971 report; see OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.

event: A federal mineral patent for the Grass Valley claim, Mineral Survey No. 2493, is issued to George Henry Lounsbury and James Guy Lounsbury.
source: BLM General Land Office records, serial patent 50-2001-0164
notes: The patent number matches the number printed on the USMS 2493 plat. No copy of the patent is saved in this repo yet; the date and names are from the BLM web record as read on 23 Nov 2026.

event: A second Lamont crew installs a sister station at Charters Towers, Australia (CTA). The report says "The tunnel was originally a gold mine that, during World War II, was enlarged and reshored for use as a munitions storage area." Lamont crew: George P. Hade Jr., John M. W. Rynn and George Choy.
source: Lamont 1971, Charters Towers station installation report (DTIC AD0729901)
locator: report p. 2 (PDF p. 9); report p. 3 (PDF p. 10)
notes: Whole report read. Both pages checked by eye. The dates overlap the Fairbanks installation of 17 Aug to 26 Sep 1970. Local staff named in the report are left out.

event: Lamont installs a sister station at Chiang Mai, Thailand (CHG), in a new concrete surface vault built in a shallow quarry. Lamont crew: George P. Hade Jr. and Andrew J. Murphy. Murphy is also named on the Fairbanks crew.
source: Lamont 1971, Chiang Mai station installation report (DTIC AD0729898)
locator: report p. 2 (PDF p. 9); report p. 3 (PDF p. 10); vault described PDF pp. 22 and 23
notes: Whole report read. Crew and location pages checked by eye. This report does not mention Fairbanks; Murphy's place on the Fairbanks crew is from the Fairbanks report, p. 1.

event: Lamont installs a sister station at Eilat, Israel (EIL), in a tunnel built in 1968 as a geophysical observatory. Lamont crew: Merrill Conner, Tracy Johnson and Marc Sbar. Conner and Johnson are also named on the Fairbanks crew.
source: Lamont 1971, Eilat station installation report (DTIC AD0729899)
locator: report p. 1 (PDF p. 6); report p. 3 (PDF p. 8); tunnel history PDF p. 14
notes: Whole report read. Crew and location pages checked by eye. This report does not mention Fairbanks; the link is from the Fairbanks report, p. 1. The 1970 design report calls this site a mine; this later report says purpose-built tunnel.

event: Recording begins at Fairbanks: analog on 26 September 1970, digital on 27 September. The two horizontal high-gain components "were excessively noisy until 25 Jan 1971 due to problems with the seismometers and galvanometers", and the digital tapes for 18 November 1970 to 24 January 1971 are unusable because the tape recorder's power supply failed.
source: Lamont 1971, Long-Period Seismological Research Program, final report (DTIC AD0729897)
notes: Table I is printed sideways; read by eye from the page image.

event: Four of the five planned stations are in: Alaska, Australia, Israel and Thailand. The fifth, at Toledo, Spain, is late because Spanish government approval did not come until March 1971. Vault work began in early April and installation "should be completed in June, 1971."
source: Lamont 1971, Long-Period Seismological Research Program, final report (DTIC AD0729897)
notes: Whole report read; page checked by eye. The report says should, so June is a plan, not a record. A 1973 report lists Toledo (TLO) among nine working stations.

event: Lamont's final report on the installation contract says the Fairbanks station can detect surface waves from Alaskan earthquakes as small as magnitude 3.8, up to 15 degrees of arc away.
source: Lamont 1971, Long-Period Seismological Research Program, final report (DTIC AD0729897)
notes: Whole report read; page checked by eye. The report writes mb = 3.8. Based on 230 hours of records. See the row on early noise problems at Fairbanks.

event: The same report notes that the stations at Eilat and Chiang Mai are 18 to 20 degrees of arc from "locations of presumed underground explosions" in Russia and China, and that two presumed Russian explosions were recorded at Eilat.
source: Lamont 1971, Long-Period Seismological Research Program, final report (DTIC AD0729897)
locator: report p. 11 (PDF p. 17); report p. 13 (PDF p. 19)
notes: Whole report read; p. 11 checked by eye. The report gives the stated purpose of the five stations as "testing this equipment under different environmental conditions" (report p. 2). It does not say they were built to watch those tests. Keep this wording.

event: In a one month test, the International Seismic Month, nine stations together detect 465 of 840 listed events. Fairbanks (FBK) detects 170. Lamont writes that five stations, Fairbanks among them, "are responsible for more than 90% of the 465 observed events." Fairbanks has the least masking of the nine, 16.4 percent.
source: Lamont 1973, Long-Period Seismological Research Program (DTIC AD0778950)
locator: report p. 6 (PDF p. 12); report p. 7 (PDF p. 13); report p. 8 (PDF p. 14); Figure 3a (PDF p. 27)
notes: Whole report read; all four pages checked by eye. The list was preliminary and the count was made by eye from paper records. Other stations detected more: Albuquerque 247, Charters Towers 240, Ogdensburg 222. The 1974 annual report (DTIC AD0784837, report p. 6) says the final list had 996 entries, and it does not repeat the five-station sentence. So this row rests on the preliminary analysis only.

event: Lamont hands the upkeep of the high-gain stations to the NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) group at Albuquerque, New Mexico. From 1 September 1972 that group copies and forwards the data tapes.
source: Lamont 1972, Long Period Seismological Research Program (DTIC AD0751960)
locator: report p. 1 (PDF p. 7); report p. 2 (PDF p. 8); report p. 3 (PDF p. 9)
notes: Whole report read; p. 2 checked by eye. The report does not date the handover more closely than this.

event: At the Ogdensburg, New Jersey observatory: "From October 1975 we have operated the station with one technician (M. Connor) and have discontinued recording seismic data from levels others than the -560 m level of the mine".
source: Lamont 1975, Long-Period Seismological Research Program (DTIC ADA108522)
notes: Whole report read; page checked by eye. The report gives no first name. Do not say this is Merrill Conner of the Fairbanks crew; that is our inference; see OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.

event: John Mikely drives the north drift of the Clipper vein ahead about 25 ft as annual assessment work, and starts a lower crosscut tunnel.
source: Territory of Alaska Mining Department, report on lode mining in the Interior of Alaska in 1932 (DGGS Miscellaneous Report 194-4; cited in OFR 157 as Pilgrim)
notes: Page checked by eye, 28 Nov 2026. The page does not name Lounsbury. Our reading, not proven: Mikely is the John Michaely listed as an owner by Reed in 1938.

event: A territorial report lists seven owners of the Clipper Mine and says "It is under lease to Lloyd P. Lounsbury." He is driving a tunnel about 200 ft long, with a Blake type jaw crusher and a 10-ton Straub ball mill on the property. "No men are employed. All mine work is done by hand."
source: Reed, Lode Mining and Development in the Year 1938, the Fairbanks District, Alaska, Territory of Alaska Department of Mines (DGGS Miscellaneous Report 194-6)
notes: Pages checked by eye, 28 Nov 2026. Owners as printed: Jos. A. McDonald, "Shorty" (D. L.) Thomas, John Michaely, Jas. McCann, Albert Bernard, Chris Foss and Peter Delasto. The typescript is faint; the initials D. L. and the first letter of Peter are uncertain. Conflict: the Reported row for 1932 calls Lloyd Lounsbury the owner. Both are kept. See OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.

event: The sixth high-gain station is installed at Toledo, Spain, in a newly excavated tunnel about 4 km from the Toledo Geophysical Observatory. Its code is TLO. The report cites the installation report as "Cory, S.E., High-gain, long-period seismograph station installation report, Toledo, Spain," Lamont-Doherty, April 1972.
source: Lamont 1972, annual report (DTIC AD0744130)
locator: report p. 6 (PDF p. 12); References, report p. 17 (PDF p. 23)
notes: Both pages checked by eye, 28 Nov 2026. No copy of the Toledo installation report has been found. Whether S.E. Cory is the Shannon Cory of the 1970 Fairbanks crew is in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.

event: The Cipher tape deck in the Fairbanks digital recorder fails on 22 August 1971. A special maintenance trip of about one week follows, and the system is repaired on 30 October 1971.
source: Lamont 1972, annual report (DTIC AD0744130)
notes: Both pages checked by eye, 28 Nov 2026. The scan prints FBK; the machine-read text had misread it as PBK. Earlier in 1971 a maintenance trip had installed an uninterruptable power unit at each site (report pp. 3 to 4).

event: A Lamont report says the experiment at Ogdensburg, New Jersey "indicates that horizontal-component seismometers should be placed at depths of 150 to 200m below the surface at a hard rock site to minimize the effects of moderate winds and atmospheric turbulence." Vertical seismometers can be run "at substantially shallower depths."
source: Lamont 1973, Long-Period Seismological Research Program, semi-annual report (DTIC AD0778950)
notes: Page checked by eye, 28 Nov 2026. The passage does not name Fairbanks. The Fairbanks station sat beneath 20 m of overburden (see the 1970 row). What this may mean for Fairbanks is our reading, in OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.
